stops.name: The Rice (Rice Hotel)
stops.teaser: A hotel built on the spot where Texas once had its capitol.
stops.map: The Rice, 909 Texas Ave, Houston, TX
stops.clue: Go to Texas Avenue between Travis and Main Streets. Look for the tall, tan building made of two tall wings, with a flat top.
stops.safety: Texas Avenue has traffic and light rail. Use crosswalks, and remember this is now an apartment building, so stay on the sidewalk.

story: The Rice stands at 909 Texas Avenue in downtown Houston, and it is the third building on its site. The Republic of Texas used the first building as its capitol from 1837 to 1839, and again from 1842 to 1845. It then became the Capitol Hotel.

In 1881 a five-story hotel replaced it. William Marsh Rice bought it in 1886, and after he died in 1900 it passed to the Rice Institute. Jesse H. Jones built the current seventeen-story, double-winged building in 1913 at a cost of about $3.5 million.

In 1922 the hotel's cafeteria became the first public room in Houston with air-conditioning. The hotel closed in 1977, stood empty for twenty-one years, and reopened in 1998 as apartments called the Post Rice Lofts. Since 2014 it has been called simply The Rice.
stops.fact: It had Houston's first air-conditioned public room.
stops.disputed: Many people think a hotel building is only ever a hotel. Wikipedia says this one began as a government capitol.

claims.t: The current Rice Hotel building was completed in 1913.
The hotel has always been a hotel and nothing else.
claims.why: It was a capitol first, then a hotel, and today it is apartments.

spot.q: The Rice reopened in 1998 as apartments after closing in 1977. About how long did the building stand empty in between?
spot.why: The hotel closed in 1977 and reopened in 1998, so it stood empty for twenty-one years.

stops.teaser: A park where four different city halls and markets used to stand.

stops.clue: Go to the park bounded by Travis and Milam Streets and Congress and Preston Avenues. Look for a green square with oak trees, a brick path and a tall metal sculpture.

story: The square was first called Congress Square in the original survey of Houston. It was renamed Market Square in 1837. The city commissioned its first market house and city hall here in 1840, and both were finished in 1841.

In 1854 Augustus Allen donated the square to the city, which used it as an open-air produce market. Several city halls rose and fell here, mostly because of fires. The fourth one, designed by George E. Dickey, was built in 1904 after a fire in 1901.
Today the square is a public park surrounded by nineteenth-century buildings and modern towers, with restaurants and bars. Market Square Tower, a 43-floor tower, opened in 2017.
stops.fact: Fires kept destroying the city halls.
stops.disputed: Many people think a city hall is built once. Wikipedia says four were built here, and several were destroyed by fire.

claims.t: The first market house on the square was finished in 1841.
claims.why: Wikipedia: both buildings were completed the year after the 1840 commission, in 1841.

claims.t: The square has always been a park.
claims.why: It was a marketplace and the site of city halls.

spot.q: The 1895 snowy photo shows an earlier city hall. The fourth one, designed by George E. Dickey, went up in 1904 after a fire. How many years before that did the fire happen?
spot.why: The fire was in 1901 and the fourth city hall was built in 1904, three years later.

stops.name: Union Station
stops.teaser: A grand 1911 train station that now sits inside a baseball park.
stops.map: Union Station, 501 Crawford St, Houston, TX
stops.clue: Go to the baseball park downtown, at Crawford and Texas Streets. Look for the old brick-and-stone station building attached to it.
stops.safety: This is a busy district, especially on game days. Use crosswalks, stay out of the traffic, and check hours before going in.

story: In 1909 the Houston Belt and Terminal Railway Company hired Warren and Wetmore to design a new union station. Several buildings had to be torn down to make room, including a house and a synagogue.

It was meant to cost $1 million, and it ended up costing about five times that. The outside is granite, limestone and terracotta, and the inside used a lot of marble. It was dedicated in March 1911, and two more floors were added the next year.

At the time Houston, with seventeen railways, was considered the main railroad hub of the southern United States. Today the building is a cornerstone of the baseball park, and Houston's Amtrak station has replaced it.
stops.fact: The station cost five times more than planned.
stops.disputed: Many people think the station is still used for trains. Wikipedia says it has been superseded by Houston's Amtrak station.

claims.t: Union Station was built to cost about $5 million.
claims.why: The estimate was $1 million. The real cost was about five times that.

spot.q: Union Station was meant to cost $1 million. About how much did it end up costing?
spot.why: It ended up costing about five times the planned $1 million.

stops.name: Cotton Exchange Building
stops.teaser: A red-brick building where cotton prices were decided.
stops.map: Cotton Exchange Building, 202 Travis St, Houston, TX
stops.clue: Go to the corner of Travis and Franklin Streets. Look for an ornate red-brick building with lots of decorative brick and an arched entrance.
stops.safety: Downtown streets are busy. Use crosswalks, and view the building from the public sidewalk.

story: The Houston Cotton Exchange and Board of Trade hired local architect Eugene Heiner to design a three-story building at the corner of Travis and Franklin. It was built in 1884.
In 1907 the building was remodeled and a fourth floor was added. The Houston Cotton Exchange kept using it until 1924, when it moved to a new building at Prairie and Caroline.
In 1973 John Hannah and Jesse Edmundson III bought the building and restored it. They sold it in 1983. The building is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
stops.disputed: Many people think the building has always had four floors. Wikipedia says it began with three.

claims.t: The Cotton Exchange Building was built in 1884.
The building has always had four floors.
claims.why: The fourth floor was added in 1907.

spot.q: The 1907 postcard shows the remodeled Cotton Exchange with a fourth floor added. How many floors did the 1884 building have?
spot.why: Eugene Heiner designed a three-story building in 1884, and the fourth floor came with the 1907 remodel.
